subject: Communication
title: Thomas-Kilmann's Five Conflict Styles
description: A short lesson to help you apply Thomas-Kilmann's Five Conflict Styles.

hook.text: When conflict arises, some people fight. Some flee. Some fold. Some negotiate. Some collaborate. Which are you?

buildup.text: Thomas and Kilmann identified five styles: Competing, Avoiding, Accommodating, Compromising, and Collaborating.

discovery.text: Each style balances two dimensions: assertiveness (your needs) and cooperativeness (their needs).

twist.text: No style is universally best. Competing works in emergencies. Avoiding works when issues are trivial.

climax.text: Most people default to one style in all situations. Mastery means choosing the right style for each conflict.

punchline.text: Conflict style isn't personality. It's a choice — if you know your options.

quiz.question: How many conflict styles did Thomas and Kilmann identify?

details.summary: The Thomas-Kilmann model identifies five conflict-handling styles based on assertiveness and cooperativeness: competing, collaborating, compromising, avoiding, and accommodating. No style is universally best; effectiveness depends on the situation and stakes involved.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding your default conflict style reveals blind spots and gives you access to four other approaches you might be neglecting.
takeaways: Five styles: competing, collaborating, compromising, avoiding, accommodating
Each style suits different situations and stakes
Most people overuse one or two styles by default

faq.question: Which conflict style is most effective overall?
faq.answer: Collaboration produces the best outcomes when time and trust allow, but it requires the most effort. Competing is best for emergencies, avoiding works for trivial issues, accommodating preserves relationships, and compromising finds quick middle ground under time pressure.

faq.question: Can you change your default conflict style?
faq.answer: Yes. The first step is awareness through self-assessment. Then practice underused styles in low-stakes situations. For example, a habitual avoider can practice competing in minor disagreements to build the skill before high-stakes moments arrive.
